<script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w21">{"year":2,"week":21,"id":"y2w21","title":"Data Project: Collection, Analysis and Interpretation","subtitle":"Planning and carrying out a mini-project on a real issue in the school or community; writing a project plan; collecting and organising data in a spreadsheet; summarising by group with averages, percentages and two-way tables; scatter graphs and correlation; drawing careful conclusions and recommendations; and presenting and publishing a report.","family":"data","section":{"no":8,"name":"Working with Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":22},"outcomes":["Write a project plan with a clear question, method, instrument, sample, ethics and timeline.","Organise collected data in a table or spreadsheet and summarise it by group.","Use averages, percentages, two-way tables, charts and scatter graphs to analyse data.","Draw conclusions and recommendations, and state the limitations of the study.","Present and publish findings in a report, slides or an infographic."],"keywords":["project","research question","hypothesis","population","sample","instrument","pilot","consent","timeline","spreadsheet","AVERAGEIF","COUNTIF","two-way table","scatter graph","correlation","line of best fit","conclusion","recommendation","limitation","infographic","report"],"notes":[{"title":"Why do a data project?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Real problems in our schools and communities, such as health, sanitation, unemployment or poor results, need **evidence**. A few complaints are not enough: data from enough people shows whether a problem is real, how big it is and who is most affected. National bodies such as the Ghana Statistical Service collect data on malaria, population and living standards so that money and services go where they are most needed."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-stages","caption":"The eight stages of a mini data project."}],"figs":["w21-stages"]},{"title":"Writing a project plan","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"A project plan answers","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Topic and aim:** what issue, and why does it matter?","**Research question(s):** for example \"Is there a link between study time and maths grades?\" You may state a **hypothesis**: \"Students who study more get better grades.\"","**Population and sample:** who the question is about, and who you will actually ask (aim for 20–50 people; choose them fairly, Week 9).","**Method and instrument:** questionnaire, interview guide or observation guide, piloted first.","**Ethics:** consent, anonymity, honesty and respect for culture.","**Timeline and budget:** when each stage happens and what it costs."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Organising the data","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Enter every response as one **row** of a spreadsheet, with one **column** per question. Spreadsheet functions summarise the data quickly:"},{"k":"ul","items":["`=AVERAGE(D2:D31)` finds the mean of a column.","`=AVERAGEIF(B2:B31,\"Female\",D2:D31)` finds the mean for one group only.","`=COUNTIF(H2:H31,\"A\")` counts how many A grades there are.","`=COUNTIFS(B2:B31,\"Male\",H2:H31,\"A\")` counts males with grade A.","`=MEDIAN(D2:D31)` and `=STDEV.P(D2:D31)` give the median and standard deviation.","`=CORREL(D2:D31,I2:I31)` measures the strength of a linear relationship (from $-1$ to $1$)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Analysing and comparing groups","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Averages and spread** for each group (Week 11).","**Percentages** to compare groups of different sizes.","**Two-way tables** to count two features at once, such as gender and grade.","**Charts:** bar charts to compare groups, pie or waffle charts for parts of a whole (Week 10)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Scatter graphs and correlation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **scatter graph** plots two numerical variables for each person. If the points rise from left to right there is a **positive correlation**; if they fall, a **negative correlation**; if there is no pattern, **no correlation**. A **line of best fit** passes through the **mean point** $(\\bar x,\\bar y)$ and follows the trend."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Correlation is not causation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A link between two variables does not prove that one causes the other. Students who study more might also have more support at home. Also, do not use a line of best fit far outside the range of the data (extrapolation)."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Conclusions, limitations and recommendations","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A **conclusion** answers the research question using the evidence, with numbers.","**Limitations** are honest weaknesses: a small or unrepresentative sample, self-reported answers, a short time period.","**Recommendations** say what should be done, by whom, based on the findings."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Presenting and publishing","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A good **report** has a title, introduction (aim and question), method, results (tables and charts), discussion (conclusions and limitations), recommendations and an appendix (the instrument). Findings can also be shared as **slides**, an **infographic** (key numbers and simple charts on one page), or published in a school magazine, a newspaper such as the *Junior Graphic*, on local radio or on social media, always protecting the privacy of the people who took part."}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"A project plan","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write an outline plan for a project on \"Why do some students arrive late to school?\""}],"steps":["**Aim:** to find the main causes of lateness and suggest solutions.","**Questions:** How far do late students travel? What transport do they use? What time do they leave home?","**Sample:** 40 students, 10 from each form level, chosen at random from the register; plus 3 teachers on duty.","**Instrument:** a short anonymous questionnaire (piloted with 5 students) and an observation tally at the gate for one week.","**Ethics and timeline:** explain the purpose, ask for consent, no names; week 1 design and pilot, week 2 collect, week 3 analyse and report."],"answer":"Aim, questions, sample, instrument, ethics and timeline stated","figs":[]},{"title":"Averages by group","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Ten students reported their weekly study hours: males 5, 3, 2, 6, 4; females 10, 8, 7, 9, 5. Compare the groups using the mean and median, and give the spreadsheet formula for the female mean."}],"steps":["Male mean $=\\dfrac{20}{5}=4$ h; female mean $=\\dfrac{39}{5}=7.8$ h.","Medians: males (2, 3, 4, 5, 6) 4 h; females (5, 7, 8, 9, 10) 8 h.","Both averages show the females in this sample study about twice as long.","Formula: `=AVERAGEIF(B2:B11,\"Female\",D2:D11)`, where column B holds gender and column D holds hours."],"answer":"Males 4 h, females 7.8 h (medians 4 h and 8 h)","figs":[]},{"title":"A two-way table","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The maths grades of the same students were: females A, B, A, A, A; males B, C, C, B, B. Make a two-way table and comment."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-gender","caption":"Mean hours and grades by gender."}],"steps":["1.",{"table":{"k":"table","head":["","A","B","C","Total"],"rows":[["female","4","1","0","5"],["male","0","3","2","5"],["total","4","4","2","10"]]}},"80% of the females but none of the males scored A; 40% of the males scored C.","With only 10 students, this is a pattern to investigate further, not proof of a difference between genders."],"answer":"Females: 4 A, 1 B; males: 3 B, 2 C","figs":["w21-gender"]},{"title":"Pie chart of shares","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Show the share of the total study hours (20 for males, 39 for females) on a pie chart."}],"steps":["Total $=59$ hours.","Males: $\\tfrac{20}{59}\\times360^\\circ\\approx122^\\circ$ (about 34%).","Females: $\\tfrac{39}{59}\\times360^\\circ\\approx238^\\circ$ (about 66%)."],"answer":"$122^\\circ$ (34%) and $238^\\circ$ (66%)","figs":[]},{"title":"Scatter graph and correlation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The study hours and self-assessment scores (out of 10) of the ten students were (5, 7), (10, 9), (3, 5), (8, 8), (2, 6), (7, 8), (6, 7), (9, 9), (4, 6), (5, 8). Describe the relationship."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-scatter","caption":"Study hours against self-assessment."}],"steps":["The points rise from left to right: a **positive correlation**. (The spreadsheet gives `=CORREL(...)`$\\approx0.90$, a strong link.)","Mean point: $\\bar x=\\tfrac{59}{10}=5.9$, $\\ \\bar y=\\tfrac{73}{10}=7.3$; the line of best fit passes through $(5.9,\\,7.3)$.","Students who study more tend to rate their understanding higher, but this does not prove that studying causes the higher rating."],"answer":"Strong positive correlation; mean point $(5.9,\\,7.3)$","figs":["w21-scatter"]},{"title":"Interpreting a published table","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The table shows the number of children aged 6–59 months **tested** for malaria by rapid diagnostic test in a 2019 survey (Sept–Nov, total 2843). Northern Region had 509, Greater Accra 186, and the monthly totals were 195, 1546 and 1102. Interpret the data, and explain what you would need before concluding which region has the **most malaria**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-malaria","caption":"Children tested for malaria by region, 2019."}],"steps":["Northern had the most children tested, $\\tfrac{509}{2843}\\approx17.9\\%$ of the total; Greater Accra the fewest, about 6.5%.","October accounts for $\\tfrac{1546}{2843}\\approx54\\%$ of all tests.","But the table counts children **tested**, not children found **positive**. To compare malaria levels, we need the number who tested positive in each region, as a **percentage of those tested** (the positivity rate).","A large count may simply mean a larger sample, so always read the title of a table carefully."],"answer":"Northern tested most (17.9%); positivity rates are needed to compare malaria levels","figs":["w21-malaria"]},{"title":"Conclusions and limitations","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write a conclusion, two limitations and two recommendations for the study-habits survey of 10 students."}],"steps":["**Conclusion:** in this sample, students who studied more hours reported higher understanding (strong positive correlation), and the females studied about twice as long as the males and obtained more A grades.","**Limitations:** only 10 students, not chosen at random; the hours and self-assessment are self-reported and may be inaccurate.","**Recommendations:** repeat the survey with a stratified random sample of at least 50 students; the school could organise supervised study groups and track whether grades improve."],"answer":"Conclusion with evidence; How often do they attend school?","**Sample:** about 40 SHS students from the community (stratified by form), plus 10 parents and 3 teachers.","**Instruments:** an anonymous questionnaire for students, an interview guide for parents and teachers; pilot both.","**Analysis:** compare the averages (for example study hours, attendance) of students with high and low grades; two-way tables of factors against grades; scatter graph of study hours against marks.","**Report:** conclusions with evidence, limitations, recommendations (such as community study centres), presented at a parents' meeting."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A neighbourhood suffers from pollution and poor waste management. Design the data collection for a project on residents' awareness and practices, and explain how you would analyse it.","steps":["**Questionnaire** for about 50 households (one adult each, chosen systematically along each street): how waste is stored and disposed of, how often it is collected, whether they separate plastics, whether they know of recycling points.","**Observation guide:** count open dumps, blocked gutters and burning sites on each street over one week.","**Analysis:** percentages for each disposal method (waffle or bar chart), a two-way table of awareness against practice, and a map or table of observed dump sites. Conclusions should be linked to the evidence, for example \"65% burn plastic waste because there is no collection\"."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Explain why the conclusion \"Northern Region has the most malaria\" cannot be drawn from a table of the number of children tested in each region. What extra data are needed?","steps":["The table counts children **tested**, which depends on how many children were sampled in each region, not on how many were infected. A region with more children tested will show a larger number even if malaria is less common there.","To compare malaria levels we need the number of children who tested **positive** in each region, and the **positivity rate** $=\\dfrac{\\text{positive}}{\\text{tested}}\\times100\\%$. To compare burden we would also need each region's population of young children."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A student finds a strong positive correlation between the number of hours students spend on social media and the number of friends they report. She concludes that \"using social media makes you more popular\". Criticise this conclusion and suggest a better one.","steps":["Correlation shows only that the two variables tend to rise together. The cause could run the other way (students with many friends spend more time chatting online), or a third factor could affect both (for example owning a smartphone). The data are also self-reported, and \"number of friends\" is hard to measure.","A better conclusion: \"In this sample, students who spent more time on social media tended to report more friends. Further study is needed to find out why.\""],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"List the sections of a good project report and say what each should contain.","steps":["**Title** that states the An **event** $E$ is a set of outcomes. When the outcomes are equally likely,"},{"k":"math","tex":"P(E)=\\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}=\\frac{\\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\\text{total number of outcomes}}"},{"k":"ul","items":["$0\\le P(E)\\le1$: 0 means impossible, 1 means certain.","**Complement:** $P(\\text{not }E)=1-P(E)$.","A probability can be written as a fraction ($\\tfrac14$), a decimal (0.25), a percentage (25%) or as a ratio of favourable to total outcomes (1 : 4)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Compound experiments","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **compound experiment** combines two or more simple experiments, such as rolling two dice or tossing a coin and rolling a die. If one experiment has $m$ outcomes and the other $k$, together they have $m\\times k$ outcomes (the **counting principle**). Show the sample space by **listing**, a **table** or a **tree diagram**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-dice","caption":"The 36 outcomes of rolling two dice."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-coindie","caption":"A tree diagram for a coin and a die."}],"figs":["w22-dice","w22-coindie"]},{"title":"Independent events","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Events are **independent** if one happening does not change the probability of the other (two coin tosses, a coin and a die)."},{"k":"math","tex":"P(A\\text{ and }B)=P(A)\\times P(B)"}],"figs":[]},{"title":"\"Or\": the addition rule","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"P(A\\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\\text{ and }B)"},{"k":"p","text":"Subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice. If $A$ and $B$ cannot happen together (**mutually exclusive**), $P(A\\text{ and }B)=0$ and $P(A\\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B)$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Dependent events","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Events are **dependent** if the first changes the probability of the second, as when items are taken **without replacement**."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Multiplication rule for dependent events","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"P(A\\text{ and }B)=P(A)\\times P(B\\mid A)"},{"k":"p","text":"$P(B\\mid A)$, read \"the probability of $B$ **given** $A$\", is the probability of $B$ after $A$ has happened. After one item is removed, both the number of favourable items and the total may change."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-tree","caption":"A tree diagram for drawing without replacement."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Using a tree diagram","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Write the probability on each branch; the branches from one point add up to 1.","**Multiply along** a path to get the probability of that outcome.","**Add** the probabilities of all the paths that give the event you want.","Check: the probabilities of all the end outcomes add up to 1."]}]}],"figs":["w22-tree"]},{"title":"Conditional probability","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Rearranging the multiplication rule gives"},{"k":"math","tex":"P(B\\mid A)=\\frac{P(A\\text{ and }B)}{P(A)}=\\frac{n(A\\cap B)}{n(A)}"},{"k":"p","text":"Knowing that $A$ has happened shrinks the sample space to $A$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-venn","caption":"Given $V$, only the students in $V$ count."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Testing independence","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$A$ and $B$ are independent exactly when $P(B\\mid A)=P(B)$, or equivalently $P(A\\text{ and }B)=P(A)\\times P(B)$. If the probabilities differ, the events are dependent."}]}],"figs":["w22-venn"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Simple experiments","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A fair die is rolled. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y3w01">{"year":3,"week":1,"id":"y3w01","title":"Logical Reasoning I: Statements, Connectives and Symbolic Logic","subtitle":"What logical reasoning is; interrogative and declarative sentences; statements, open sentences and opinions; truth values; negation, including statements with “all”, “some” and “no”; conjunctions and disjunctions in symbols; implications shown with Venn diagrams; testing conclusions and finding counterexamples; and logic in robotics, computing, law and decision-making.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Logical Reasoning and Variation","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":5},"outcomes":["Explain logical reasoning and distinguish deductive from inductive reasoning.","Change interrogative sentences into declarative statements and classify statements as true, false or debatable.","Write the negation of simple and quantified statements in words and in symbols.","Form conjunctions $p\\wedge q$ and disjunctions $p\\vee q$ and find their truth values.","Represent implications such as “all $P$ are $Q$” on Venn diagrams and decide whether conclusions are valid.","Apply symbolic logic to real-world situations such as logic gates, rules and simple decisions."],"keywords":["logical reasoning","deductive reasoning","inductive reasoning","declarative statement","interrogative sentence","statement","open sentence","truth value","debatable","negation","quantifier","conjunction","disjunction","compound statement","implication","counterexample","Venn diagram","valid conclusion","logic gate"],"notes":[{"title":"What is logical reasoning?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Logical reasoning** is the systematic process of reaching conclusions, making decisions or solving problems from the facts and evidence available, using clear rules. It is the foundation of mathematical thinking: we use rules, look for patterns, analyse information and make sound judgements."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Two kinds of reasoning","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Deductive reasoning** starts from general facts that are accepted as true and reaches a conclusion that **must** follow. *All mammals breathe air; a goat is a mammal; so a goat breathes air.*","**Inductive reasoning** looks at particular cases, notices a pattern and makes a general guess. *$1+3=4$, $1+3+5=9$, $1+3+5+7=16$, so the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers seems to be $n^2$.* An inductive conclusion is likely, but it is not proved until it is shown deductively."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Sentences and statements","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Type of sentence","Example","A statement?"],"rows":[["interrogative (asks)","“Is Accra the capital of Ghana?”","no"],["imperative (commands)","“Close the door.”","no"],["exclamatory","“What a goal!”","no"],["declarative (tells)","“Accra is the capital of Ghana.”","yes"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Statement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **statement** (or proposition) is a declarative sentence that is either **true** or **false**, but not both. Its **truth value** is T (true) or F (false)."}]},{"k":"ul","items":["An **open sentence** such as $x+2=5$ is neither true nor false until $x$ is known; it is true only for $x=3$.","An **opinion** such as “Mathematics is more important than Robotics” depends on the person: we call it **debatable**.","A statement about the real world is decided by **evidence**; a mathematical statement is decided by **proof** or by a **counterexample**."]},{"k":"p","text":"We name statements with capital or small letters: $p$: *2 is an even number*."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Negation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **negation** of a statement $p$, written $\\sim p$ (read “not $p$”), has the **opposite** truth value: if $p$ is true, $\\sim p$ is false, and if $p$ is false, $\\sim p$ is true."},{"k":"table","head":["$p$","$\\sim p$"],"rows":[["T","F"],["F","T"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Negating “all”, “some” and “no”","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The words **all**, **some** and **no** are called **quantifiers**. To negate them correctly:"},{"k":"ul","items":["“All $A$ are $B$” is negated by “**Some** $A$ are **not** $B$.”","“Some $A$ are $B$” is negated by “**No** $A$ is $B$.”","“No $A$ is $B$” is negated by “**Some** $A$ are $B$.”"]},{"k":"p","text":"So the negation of “All prime numbers are odd” is “Some prime numbers are not odd” (true: 2), **not** “All prime numbers are even”."}]},{"k":"p","text":"For inequalities: the negation of $x\\le10$ is $x>10$, and the negation of $x>5$ is $x\\le5$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Conjunctions and disjunctions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **simple statement** carries one idea. **Connectives** such as *and*, *or*, *not* and *if … then* join simple statements into **compound statements**."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Conjunction and disjunction","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **conjunction** $p\\wedge q$ means “$p$ **and** $q$”. It is true **only when both** $p$ and $q$ are true.","The **disjunction** $p\\vee q$ means “$p$ **or** $q$” (or both). It is true when **at least one** of $p$, $q$ is true; it is false only when both are false."]},{"k":"p","text":"(Some books, including the Teacher Manual, draw $\\wedge$ and $\\vee$ as ⋏ and ⋎.)"}]},{"k":"table","head":["$p$","$q$","$p\\wedge q$","$p\\vee q$"],"rows":[["T","T","T","T"],["T","F","F","T"],["F","T","F","T"],["F","F","F","F"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"note","title":"Inclusive and exclusive “or”","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In mathematics “or” is **inclusive**: “$p$ or $q$” is true when both are true. In everyday speech “tea or coffee?” usually means one but not both; that is the **exclusive or**."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Implications and Venn diagrams","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"“If $p$, then $q$” is written $p\\Rightarrow q$ and read “$p$ implies $q$”. A statement such as “All $P$ are $Q$” is an implication: *if a thing is in $P$, then it is in $Q$*. On a Venn diagram, $P$ is drawn **inside** $Q$ ($P\\subset Q$)."},{"k":"fig","id":"w01-subset","caption":"“All $P$ are $Q$” means $P\\subset Q$; similarly $x>5\\Rightarrow x>3$."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Testing a conclusion","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A conclusion is **valid** if it **must** be true whenever the given statements are true: the diagram leaves no other possibility.","A conclusion is **not valid** if the diagram allows a case where it fails.","To show that a general statement is false, one **counterexample** is enough.","$p\\Rightarrow q$ does **not** mean $q\\Rightarrow p$: “all students are critical thinkers” does not mean “all critical thinkers are students”."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Logic in the real world","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Robotics and computing:** circuits are built from AND, OR and NOT gates, and programs follow *if … then* rules.","**Game design and artificial intelligence:** characters and chatbots choose actions by testing conditions.","**Law:** judges check whether the evidence makes a conclusion certain, likely or impossible.","**Daily decisions:** “If it rains **and** the road is flooded, I will take the bus” is a compound condition."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w01-gates","caption":"The three basic logic gates and their truth tables."}],"figs":["w01-subset","w01-gates"]}],"examples":[{"title":"From questions to statements","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Change each interrogative sentence into a declarative statement: (a) “Is Accra the capital of Ghana?” (b) “Will Ghana win the next World Cup?” (c) “Does success not depend on corruption?” (d) “Can geometric construction be done without a compass?”"}],"steps":["(a) Accra is the capital of Ghana.","(b) Ghana will win the next World Cup.","(c) Success does not depend on corruption.","(d) Geometric construction can be done without a compass.","Each is now a declarative sentence ending with a full stop, so it can be judged true, false or debatable."],"answer":"(a) Accra is the capital of Ghana. (b) Ghana will win the next World Cup. (c) Success does not depend on corruption. (d) Geometric construction can be done without a compass.","figs":[]},{"title":"Statement or not?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Which of these are statements? For each statement, give its truth value. (a) $7$ is a prime number. (b) Solve $3x=12$. (c) $x+4=9$. (d) Every square is a rectangle. (e) Is $\\sqrt2$ rational?"}],"steps":["(a) A statement, true: the only factors of 7 are 1 and 7.","(b) An imperative sentence (a command): not a statement.","(c) An open sentence: true only when $x=5$, so on its own it is not a statement.","(d) A statement, true: a square has four right angles and opposite sides equal.","(e) An interrogative sentence: not a statement."],"answer":"Statements: (a) true, (d) true; (b), (c) and (e) are not statements","figs":[]},{"title":"True, false or debatable?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Label each as true, false or debatable, with a reason. (a) Ghana is in West Africa. (b) If $n$ is a number, then $5n>n$. (c) Ghana gained independence in 1967. (d) Mathematics is more important than Robotics. (e) If $x>5$, then $x>3$. (f) All prime numbers are odd. (g) The angles of a triangle add up to $360^\\circ$."}],"steps":["(a) True: a geographical fact.","(b) False: counterexample $n=0$ gives $0>0$, which is false; any negative $n$ also fails.","(c) False: Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957.","(d) Debatable: it is an opinion.","(e) True: every number greater than 5 is greater than 3 (Figure 1.1).","(f) False: 2 is a prime number and is even.","(g) False: the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\\circ$."],"answer":"(a) T (b) F (c) F (d) debatable (e) T (f) F (g) F","figs":[]},{"title":"Negating statements","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write the negation of each statement and state which of the pair is true. (a) $p$: $2$ is an even prime number. (b) $q$: All prime numbers are odd. (c) $r$: Some students are lazy. (d) $s$: $x\\le10$."}],"steps":["(a) $\\sim p$: 2 is not an even prime number. $p$ is true, so $\\sim p$ is false.","(b) $\\sim q$: Some prime numbers are not odd. $q$ is false, so $\\sim q$ is true (the number 2).","(c) $\\sim r$: No student is lazy. (Exactly one of $r$ and $\\sim r$ is true; which one depends on the class.)","(d) $\\sim s$: $x>10$."],"answer":"(a) “2 is not an even prime” (b) “Some prime numbers are not odd” (c) “No student is lazy” (d) $x>10$","figs":[]},{"title":"Conjunctions and disjunctions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For each pair, write $p\\wedge q$ and $p\\vee q$ in words and give their truth values. (a) $p$: 2 is an even number; $q$: 2 is an odd number. (b) $p$: Plane shapes have no volume; $q$: Solid shapes have volume."}],"steps":["(a) $p$ is true and $q$ is false.","$p\\wedge q$: 2 is an even number and 2 is an odd number. False (not both true).","$p\\vee q$: 2 is an even number or 2 is an odd number. True (at least one is true).","(b) Both $p$ and $q$ are true.","$p\\wedge q$: Plane shapes have no volume and solid shapes have volume. True.","$p\\vee q$: Plane shapes have no volume or solid shapes have volume. True — this is a true **disjunction**."],"answer":"(a) $p\\wedge q$ F, $p\\vee q$ T (b) both T","figs":[]},{"title":"More compound statements","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Write a conjunction and a disjunction for each pair and state whether each is true or false. (a) $M$: Factors divide a given number. $N$: All factors are composite numbers. (b) $S$: For $x\\ge9$, $x$ is a negative integer. $T$: For $x\\ge9$, $x$ is a factor of 3. (c) $G$: Mappings have rules. $H$: Mappings have ordered pairs."}],"steps":["(a) $M$ is true. $N$ is false: 1 and the prime factors (for example 2 is a factor of 6) are not composite. So $M\\wedge N$ is F and $M\\vee N$ is T.","(b) $S$ is false (numbers $\\ge9$ are positive). $T$ is false (the factors of 3 are 1 and 3, both less than 9). So $S\\wedge T$ is F and $S\\vee T$ is F.","(c) $G$ and $H$ are both true, so $G\\wedge H$ is T and $G\\vee H$ is T."],"answer":"(a) F, T (b) F, F (c) T, T","figs":[]},{"title":"An implication and its converse","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Is “If $x>5$, then $x>3$” true? Is the reversed statement “If $x>3$, then $x>5$” true?"}],"steps":["Every number greater than 5 is also greater than 3: on the number line the set $x>5$ lies inside $x>3$ (Figure 1.1). The implication is **true**.","The reversed statement (the **converse**) fails for $x=4$: $4>3$ but $4\\not>5$.","One counterexample is enough, so the converse is **false**."],"answer":"The implication is true; its converse is false (counterexample $x=4$).","figs":[]},{"title":"A counterexample from everyday life","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$F$: A person is bitten by a mosquito. $G$: A person gets malaria. Ntim is bitten by a mosquito but does not get malaria. Draw a Venn diagram and decide whether “$F\\Rightarrow G$” is true."}],"steps":["Let $U$ = persons, $F$ = persons bitten by mosquitoes, $G$ = persons with malaria.","Ntim belongs to $F$ but not to $G$, so $F$ is **not** inside $G$.","The implication “if a person is bitten by a mosquito, then the person gets malaria” is therefore **false**: Ntim is a counterexample.","(Only some mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite, which is why the two sets merely overlap.)"],"answer":"$F\\Rightarrow G$ is false; Ntim is a counterexample.","figs":["w01-mosquito"]},{"title":"Which conclusions are valid?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$C$: All students are critical thinkers. $D$: All students study mathematics. Using $U$ = persons, $P$ = critical thinkers, $Q$ = students and $R$ = people who study mathematics, draw a Venn diagram and decide whether each conclusion is valid. (i) Apah is a student, so Apah studies mathematics. (ii) Afoa is a critical thinker, so Afoa is a student. (iii) Quaye studies mathematics, so Quaye is a critical thinker."}],"steps":["$C$ gives $Q\\subset P$ and $D$ gives $Q\\subset R$, so $Q$ lies inside $P\\cap R$.","(i) Apah $\\in Q$ and $Q\\subset R$, so Apah $\\in R$: **valid** (true).","(ii) Afoa can be in $P$ outside $Q$: the conclusion need not hold, so it is **not valid**.","(iii) Quaye can be in $R$ outside $P$: **not valid**."],"answer":"(i) valid (ii) not valid (iii) not valid","figs":["w01-students"]},{"title":"Ghana-made cars","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$M$: Ghana-made cars are attractive. $N$: Many Ghana-made cars do not last long. Using $G$ = Ghana-made cars, $A$ = attractive cars and $L$ = cars that last long: (a) draw a Venn diagram (b) describe three regions (c) Mr Boateng’s car is attractive and lasts long. Is it Ghana-made?"}],"steps":["(a) $M$ says every Ghana-made car is attractive, so $G\\subset A$: the regions of $G$ outside $A$ (labelled $a$ and $c$ in Figure 1.5) are empty. $N$ says that part of $G$ lies outside $L$.","(b) Region $b$: Ghana-made cars that are attractive but do not last long (not empty, by $N$). Region $d$: Ghana-made cars that are attractive and last long. Region $h$: foreign cars that are neither attractive nor long-lasting.","(c) The car is in $A\\cap L$, which is region $d$ (Ghana-made) **or** region $f$ (not Ghana-made).","The statements do not tell us which, so we **cannot conclude** that the car is Ghana-made."],"answer":"(c) Not determined: the car may or may not be Ghana-made.","figs":["w01-cars"]},{"title":"Staff and holidays","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$P$: Teaching staff go on holidays. $Q$: No kitchen staff go on holidays. Using $T$ = teaching staff, $K$ = kitchen staff and $H$ = people who go on holidays, decide which conclusions are valid. (i) Mr Asiedu is kitchen staff, so he does not go on holidays. (ii) Ms Freda goes on holidays, so she is teaching staff. (iii) Anowa does not go on holidays, so Anowa is kitchen staff."}],"steps":["$P$: $T\\subset H$. $Q$: $K\\cap H=\\varnothing$.","(i) Asiedu $\\in K$ and $K$ has no members in $H$, so Asiedu $\\notin H$: **valid**.","(ii) Freda $\\in H$, but $H$ may contain people other than teachers (for example office staff): **not valid**.","(iii) Anowa $\\notin H$, but people outside $H$ need not be kitchen staff: **not valid**."],"answer":"(i) valid (ii) not valid (iii) not valid","figs":["w01-staff"]},{"title":"A chain of statements","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$K$: Being sincere is a good virtue. $L$: Good virtues are Ghanaian values. Decide whether each conclusion is definitely true, possibly true or false. (a) Auntie Rukia is a Ghanaian, so she has good virtues. (b) Uncle Mensah is very sincere, so he is a Ghanaian. (c) Kojo Baadu is sincere, so he has a Ghanaian value."}],"steps":["Let $S$ = sincere people, $V$ = people with good virtues, $W$ = people with Ghanaian values. $K$: $S\\subset V$; $L$: $V\\subset W$; so $S\\subset W$.","(a) Being Ghanaian is about nationality, not about the sets $S$, $V$ or $W$. The statements say nothing about it: **not a valid conclusion** (it reverses the logic).","(b) Having a Ghanaian value does not make a person Ghanaian; a non-Ghanaian can be sincere: **not valid**.","(c) Kojo $\\in S\\subset V\\subset W$, so Kojo $\\in W$: **definitely true**."],"answer":"(a) not valid (b) not valid (c) definitely true","figs":["w01-chain"]},{"title":"A security light","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A security light $L$ should switch on when it is dark ($d$) **and** movement is detected ($m$), **or** when the manual switch ($s$) is on. (a) Write $L$ in symbols. (b) Is the light on when it is dark, there is no movement and the switch is off? (c) Is it on at midday when the switch is on?"}],"steps":["(a) $L=(d\\wedge m)\\vee s$: an AND gate feeding an OR gate (Figure 1.2).","(b) $d$ = T, $m$ = F, $s$ = F: $d\\wedge m$ = F, then F $\\vee$ F = F. The light is **off**.","(c) $d$ = F, $m$ unknown, $s$ = T: whatever $d\\wedge m$ is, $(\\dots)\\vee$ T = T. The light is **on**."],"answer":"(a) $(d\\wedge m)\\vee s$ (b) off (c) on","figs":[]},{"title":"A farmer’s decision","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer in the Volta Region has 10 acres for maize and cassava. He wants at least 3 acres of maize and at least 2 acres of cassava. Maize yields 2 tonnes per acre and cassava 3 tonnes per acre. How should he share the land to get the greatest total yield? Justify your answer logically."}],"steps":["Let $m$ acres be maize and $c$ acres cassava: $m+c=10$, $m\\ge3$, $c\\ge2$.","Moving one acre from maize to cassava changes the yield by $3-2=+1$ tonne, so the yield increases as $c$ increases.","So $c$ should be as large as possible: $m$ is at its least value, 3, and $c=7$.","Yield $=2(3)+3(7)=6+21=27$ tonnes. Check the other extreme: $m=8$, $c=2$ gives $16+6=22$ tonnes."],"answer":"3 acres of maize and 7 acres of cassava, giving 27 tonnes","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["A statement is a declarative sentence that is true or false; open sentences and opinions are not.","$\\sim p$ has the opposite truth value of $p$. Not “all” is “some … not”; not “some” is “no”.","$p\\wedge q$ is true only when both are true; $p\\vee q$ is false only when both are false.","“All $P$ are $Q$” means $P\\subset Q$, that is $P\\Rightarrow Q$; it does not give $Q\\Rightarrow P$.","A conclusion is valid only if it must hold; one counterexample disproves a general statement."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which of these is a statement?","options":["15 is divisible by 4.","Is 15 divisible by 4?","Divide 15 by 4.","$x$ is divisible by 4."],"correct":0,"explain":"It is a declarative sentence, and it is false."},{"q":"The negation of “All mangoes are sweet” is","options":["Some mangoes are not sweet.","All mangoes are not sweet.","No mango is sweet.","Some mangoes are sweet."],"correct":0,"explain":"Not “all” means “some … not”."},{"q":"If $p$ is true and $q$ is false, then $p\\wedge q$ is","options":["false","true","debatable","both true and false"],"correct":0,"explain":"A conjunction needs both parts true."},{"q":"If $p$ is true and $q$ is false, then $p\\vee q$ is","options":["true","false","debatable","undefined"],"correct":0,"explain":"A disjunction needs at least one part true."},{"q":"$p\\vee q$ is false only when","options":["$p$ and $q$ are both false","$p$ and $q$ are both true","$p$ is true and $q$ is false","$p$ is false and $q$ is true"],"correct":0,"explain":"Otherwise at least one part is true."},{"q":"“All $A$ are $B$” is shown on a Venn diagram by","options":["$A$ drawn inside $B$","$B$ drawn inside $A$","$A$ and $B$ not overlapping","$A$ and $B$ overlapping partly"],"correct":0,"explain":"Every member of $A$ is in $B$."},{"q":"The negation of $x>5$ is","options":["$x\\le5$","$x<5$","$x\\ge5$","$x>-5$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Exactly one of $x>5$ and $x\\le5$ is true."},{"q":"Which value of $n$ is a counterexample to “$5n>n$ for every number $n$”?","options":["$n=-1$","$n=1$","$n=2$","$n=10$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$5(-1)=-5$, which is not greater than $-1$."},{"q":"“The sum of the angles of a triangle is $360^\\circ$” is","options":["false","true","debatable","not a statement"],"correct":0,"explain":"It is $180^\\circ$."},{"q":"A light is on when $(d\\wedge m)\\vee s$. Example: the angles of every triangle add to $180^\\circ$; a triangle has angles $50^\\circ$ and $60^\\circ$; so the third angle is $70^\\circ$."},{"k":"p","text":"Inductive reasoning generalises from particular cases. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y3w02">{"year":3,"week":2,"id":"y3w02","title":"Logical Reasoning II: Intelligent Guessing, Valid Arguments and Truth Tables","subtitle":"Making and testing conjectures from patterns; deciding by weighing factors; the conditional p → q and its converse, inverse and contrapositive; valid and invalid argument forms; testing arguments with truth tables; and drawing conclusions from “all”, “no” and “some” statements on Venn diagrams.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Logical Reasoning and Variation","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":5},"outcomes":["Make an intelligent guess (conjecture) from a pattern, justify it, generalise it and test it.","Use logical reasoning and simple calculations to make and defend decisions.","Construct truth tables for conditional and compound statements.","Write the converse, inverse and contrapositive of a conditional and say which are equivalent.","Distinguish valid argument forms from common fallacies.","Represent quantified statements on Venn diagrams and decide whether conclusions are valid."],"keywords":["intelligent guessing","conjecture","pattern","generalisation","triangular number","decision making","weighted score","conditional","antecedent","consequent","converse","inverse","contrapositive","biconditional","valid argument","premise","conclusion","modus ponens","modus tollens","fallacy","truth table","tautology","quantifier"],"notes":[{"title":"Intelligent guessing","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **intelligent guess** (a **conjecture**) is a prediction based on careful study of the evidence, not a wild guess. To make one from a pattern, ask useful questions:"},{"k":"ul","items":["How do successive terms behave: increasing, decreasing, alternating?","What is the nature of the change: a constant difference, a growing difference, a constant ratio?","Can the rule be written for the $n$th term, and does it reproduce every given term?"]},{"k":"p","text":"The Fibonacci numbers $1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \\dots$ are formed by adding the two previous terms, so the next term is $5+8=13$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-triangular","caption":"The triangular numbers: each new row is one dot longer."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Differences reveal the rule","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**First differences constant** (e.g. $3, 7, 11, 15$): the rule is linear, $T_n=an+b$.","**Second differences constant** (e.g. $1, 3, 6, 10$): the rule is quadratic, $T_n=an^2+bn+c$, with $2a$ equal to the second difference.","**Constant ratio** (e.g. $3, 6, 12, 24$): the rule is geometric, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"A pattern is not a proof","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A conjecture must be **tested**. Points on a circle joined by chords give $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ regions, which suggests doubling, but six points give **31** regions, not 32. One failed case destroys a conjecture; to establish it we need a deductive argument."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-circles","caption":"The doubling pattern breaks at six points."}],"figs":["w02-triangular","w02-circles"]},{"title":"Decision making","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Logical reasoning lets us use established patterns to predict outcomes and decide what to do. A sound decision:"},{"k":"ol","items":["states the goal clearly (arrive on time, earn the most, stay safe);","lists the options and the **factors** (criteria) that matter;","judges each option on each factor, using numbers where possible;","chooses the option that best meets the goal, and gives the reasons."]},{"k":"p","text":"When factors are not equally important, give each a **weight**. The weighted score of an option is"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{score}=\\sum(\\text{weight}\\times\\text{rating})."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The conditional statement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"“If $p$, then $q$” is written $p\\rightarrow q$ (or $p\\Rightarrow q$). $p$ is the **antecedent** (hypothesis) and $q$ the **consequent** (conclusion)."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Truth value of $p\\rightarrow q$","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$p\\rightarrow q$ is **false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false**. Think of it as a promise: “If you pass, I will buy you a phone.” The promise is broken only if you pass and get no phone. If you fail, the promise is not broken whatever happens."}]},{"k":"table","head":["$p$","$q$","$p\\rightarrow q$","$q\\rightarrow p$","$\\sim p\\rightarrow\\sim q$","$\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$"],"rows":[["T","T","T","T","T","T"],["T","F","F","T","T","F"],["F","T","T","F","F","T"],["F","F","T","T","T","T"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Related conditionals","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $p\\rightarrow q$:"},{"k":"ul","items":["**converse** $q\\rightarrow p$;","**inverse** $\\sim p\\rightarrow\\sim q$;","**contrapositive** $\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$."]},{"k":"p","text":"A conditional and its **contrapositive** are **equivalent** (same truth values). The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other, but **not** to the original."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **biconditional** $p\\leftrightarrow q$ (“$p$ if and only if $q$”) means $p\\rightarrow q$ **and** $q\\rightarrow p$; it is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Valid arguments","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **argument** is a set of statements called **premises** followed by a **conclusion**. An argument is **valid** if the conclusion **must** be true whenever all the premises are true. Validity is about the **form** of the argument, not about whether the premises are actually true."},{"k":"p","text":"**Valid forms**"},{"k":"table","head":["Name","Premises","Conclusion"],"rows":[["modus ponens","$p\\rightarrow q$; $p$","$q$"],["modus tollens","$p\\rightarrow q$; $\\sim q$","$\\sim p$"],["chain rule","$p\\rightarrow q$; $q\\rightarrow r$","$p\\rightarrow r$"],["disjunctive","$p\\vee q$; $\\sim p$","$q$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"**Fallacies (invalid forms)**"},{"k":"table","head":["Name","Premises","“Conclusion”"],"rows":[["affirming the consequent","$p\\rightarrow q$; $q$","$p$"],["denying the antecedent","$p\\rightarrow q$; $\\sim p$","$\\sim q$"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Testing an argument with a truth table","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["Make a column for each premise and for the conclusion.","Find the rows in which **every premise is true**.","If the conclusion is true in **all** of those rows, the argument is valid. If **one** such row has a false conclusion, it is invalid."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"A compound statement that is true in every row is a **tautology**; one that is false in every row is a **contradiction**."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Quantified statements on Venn diagrams","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w02-quantifiers","caption":"The four standard forms."},{"k":"ul","items":["“All $A$ are $B$”: draw $A$ inside $B$.","“No $A$ is $B$”: draw $A$ and $B$ apart ($A\\cap B=\\varnothing$).","“Some $A$ are $B$”: overlap them and mark the overlap as non-empty.","“Some $A$ are not $B$”: overlap them and mark the part of $A$ outside $B$."]},{"k":"p","text":"Where the statements say nothing about a region, the diagram must leave it **possible but not certain**. A conclusion is valid only if it holds in **every** diagram that fits the statements."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Where this reasoning is used","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Engineers design control systems from *if … then* rules, doctors reason from symptoms to possible causes (taking care not to affirm the consequent), lawyers test whether evidence forces a verdict, and planners weigh cost, time and safety before choosing a project."}]}],"figs":["w02-quantifiers"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Triangular numbers","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Observe the pattern $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \\dots$ (a) Guess the next three terms and justify your guess. So the next differences are $6, 7, 8$.","Next terms: $15+6=21$, $21+7=28$, $28+8=36$.","(b) The second differences are constant (1), so the rule is quadratic. Second differences: $2, 2, 2$ (constant), so $T_n=an^2+bn+c$ with $2a=2$, $a=1$.","(a) Next differences 12 and 14: terms $30+12=42$, $42+14=56$.","(b) $T_n-n^2$: $2-1=1$, $6-4=2$, $12-9=3$, so $T_n-n^2=n$ and $T_n=n^2+n=n(n+1)$.","(c) $T_{50}=50\\times51=2550$.","(d) Solve $n(n+1)=380$: $n^2+n-380=0$, $(n+20)(n-19)=0$, $n=19$. So 380 is the 19th term."],"answer":"(a) 42, 56 (b) $n(n+1)$ (c) 2550 (d) yes, $T_{19}=380$","figs":[]},{"title":"A conjecture that fails","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Mark $n$ points on a circle and join every pair with a chord, choosing the points so that no three chords meet at one point. Count the regions for $n=1$ to $5$ and make a conjecture. Then test it for $n=6$."}],"steps":["The counts are $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$ (Figure 2.2).","The pattern suggests doubling: conjecture $R_n=2^{n-1}$, which predicts $R_6=32$.","Careful counting for six points gives $31$ regions.","So the conjecture is **false**; one counterexample is enough. (The correct rule is $R_n=1+\\binom n2+\\binom n4$, which gives $1+15+15=31$.)","Lesson: an intelligent guess must be tested, and only proof makes it certain."],"answer":"Conjecture $2^{n-1}$; it fails at $n=6$ (31, not 32).","figs":[]},{"title":"Filling a tank","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A worker fills a 6400-litre tank using a 20-litre bucket. (b) If he pours in 6 buckets a day instead, how many days are saved?"}],"steps":["(a) Water added each day: $5\\times20=100$ litres. Net gain: $100-2=98$ litres per day.","$6400\\div98=65$ remainder 30: after 65 days the tank holds $65\\times98=6370$ litres, 30 litres short.","On day 66 the first two buckets ($40$ litres) fill it, so the tank is full on the **66th day** (Figure 2.4).","(b) Net gain $6\\times20-2=118$ litres per day. $6400\\div118=54$ remainder 28, so the tank is full on day 55.","Days saved: $66-55=11$."],"answer":"(a) 66 days (b) 55 days, saving 11 days","figs":["w02-tank"]},{"title":"Choosing a course","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Mary Akugiri is choosing a tertiary course under three conditions: $A$ (cost), $B$ (prospects) and $C$ (duration), shown on a Venn diagram. (a) Describe the students in region $t=A\\cap B\\cap C$. (b) Describe the students in $C\\cap(A\\cup B)'$. (c) Write in set notation “students who consider cost and prospects but not duration”."}],"steps":["(a) Region $t$ is in all three sets: these students weigh cost, prospects **and** duration before deciding.","(b) $(A\\cup B)'$ is outside both $A$ and $B$; intersecting with $C$ leaves “$C$ only”. These students consider **only** the duration of the course.","(c) In $A$ and in $B$ but outside $C$: $A\\cap B\\cap C'$."],"answer":"(a) all three conditions (b) duration only (c) $A\\cap B\\cap C'$","figs":["w02-course"]},{"title":"A weighted decision","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A candidate must travel from Goaso to Accra, partly on a dusty road, for an interview. She rates four options out of 10 and weights the factors cost 0.3, time 0.3, comfort 0.2 and safety 0.2. Which option should she choose?"},{"k":"table","head":["","Cost","Time","Comf.","Safety"],"rows":[["STC","7","7","8","8"],["Tro-tro","9","4","4","6"],["Car","3","9","9","7"],["Flight","2","8","9","9"]]},{"k":"p","text":"(“Car” is a hired private car; “Flight” goes via Kumasi.)"}],"steps":["STC: $0.3(7)+0.3(7)+0.2(8)+0.2(8)=2.1+2.1+1.6+1.6=7.4$.","Tro-tro: $2.7+1.2+0.8+1.2=5.9$.","Private car: $0.9+2.7+1.8+1.4=6.8$.","Flight: $0.6+2.4+1.8+1.8=6.6$.","STC has the highest score. It is cheaper than hiring a car or flying, more punctual and comfortable than a tro-tro, and she arrives neat and rested."],"answer":"STC (score 7.4)","figs":[]},{"title":"Where to sell farm produce","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer in the Ahafo Region has 40 bags of maize. Market women will buy them in the village at GH₵450 a bag. At the town market on market day he can get GH₵520 a bag, but transport costs GH₵35 a bag and the market toll is GH₵200. (a) Which option gives more money? (b) Below what market price would selling in the village be better? (c) Give two non-money factors he should consider."}],"steps":["(a) Village: $40\\times450=18\\,000$, so GH₵18 000.","Market: income $40\\times520=20\\,800$ (GH₵); costs $40\\times35+200=1600$ (GH₵); net GH₵19 200.","The market gives GH₵1200 more.","(b) Break-even: $40p-1600=18\\,000$, so $40p=19\\,600$ and $p=490$. If the market price falls below GH₵490 a bag, the village is better.","(c) The risk of not selling every bag at the market, the effort and stress of transport, the chance to buy goods in town, and the ability to compare prices so as not to be cheated."],"answer":"(a) market, by GH₵1200 (b) GH₵490 a bag (c) for example risk of unsold bags; access to other goods","figs":[]},{"title":"A Ludo decision","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a game of Ludo, Odeibea notices: $X$: if she throws a 6, she can capture Yaw’s marble. $Y$: if she captures it, her marble will sit where Yaw could capture it. $Z$: Yaw’s marble is vulnerable now. Yaw would need one particular number on his next throw to capture her. Should she aim to capture? Support your answer with probabilities."}],"steps":["A 6 also gives her an extra throw, and capturing sends Yaw’s marble back home, which delays him: a clear gain.","The risk is that Yaw throws the one number he needs: probability $\\dfrac16$.","So once she captures, she stays safe with probability $\\dfrac56$ (Figure 2.6).","The probability that she throws a 6 **and** then stays safe is $\\dfrac16\\times\\dfrac56=\\dfrac{5}{36}$; the risk part alone is small.","The gain is certain and the risk is small, so the logical decision is to capture."],"answer":"Yes: after capturing she is safe with probability $\\dfrac56$.","figs":["w02-ludo"]},{"title":"A truth table for $(P\\wedge Q)\\rightarrow R$","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$P$: a student attends the extra class. $Q$: the student studies at home. $R$: the student passes the test. The student says “$(P\\wedge Q)\\rightarrow R$.” (a) Construct the truth table. (b) In which case is the student’s claim false? (c) What should the student do, and does this guarantee a pass?"}],"steps":["(a)",{"table":{"k":"table","head":["$P$","$Q$","$R$","$P\\wedge Q$","$(P\\wedge Q)\\rightarrow R$"],"rows":[["T","T","T","T","T"],["T","T","F","T","F"],["T","F","T","F","T"],["T","F","F","F","T"],["F","T","T","F","T"],["F","T","F","F","T"],["F","F","T","F","T"],["F","F","F","F","T"]]}},"(b) The claim is false only in row 2: the student attends **and** studies, but fails.","(c) Attending and studying make $P\\wedge Q$ true; if the claim holds, $R$ must then be true. So the student should do both. It guarantees a pass only if the claim itself is true; the logic shows what follows from it, not that it is true."],"answer":"(b) Only when $P$ and $Q$ are true and $R$ is false. (c) Do both; the pass follows if the claim holds.","figs":[]},{"title":"Converse, inverse and contrapositive","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$p$: Madam Kukua has leadership skills. $q$: Madam Kukua heads an SHS. Given that $p\\rightarrow q$ is true, decide which statements must be true. (i) If Madam Kukua does not head an SHS, then she does not have leadership skills. (ii) If Madam Kukua heads an SHS, then she has leadership skills. (iii) If Madam Kukua has leadership skills, then she heads an SHS."}],"steps":["(i) is $\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$, the **contrapositive**. It has the same truth values as $p\\rightarrow q$, so it is true: **valid**.","(ii) is $q\\rightarrow p$, the **converse**. From the table in the Notes, $p\\rightarrow q$ can be true while $q\\rightarrow p$ is false (row 3): **not valid**.","(iii) is $p\\rightarrow q$ itself: **valid**."],"answer":"(i) valid (ii) not valid (iii) valid","figs":[]},{"title":"Valid or fallacy?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Name the form of each argument and say whether it is valid. (a) If a number ends in 0, it is divisible by 5. 340 ends in 0. So 340 is divisible by 5. (b) If it rains, the pitch is wet. The pitch is not wet. So it did not rain. (c) If Kofi studies, he passes. Kofi passed. So Kofi studied. (d) If a shape is a square, it has four sides. This shape is not a square. So it does not have four sides."}],"steps":["(a) $p\\rightarrow q$, $p$, so $q$: **modus ponens**, valid.","(b) $p\\rightarrow q$, $\\sim q$, so $\\sim p$: **modus tollens**, valid.","(c) $p\\rightarrow q$, $q$, so $p$: **affirming the consequent**, invalid. Kofi may have passed for another reason.","(d) $p\\rightarrow q$, $\\sim p$, so $\\sim q$: **denying the antecedent**, invalid. A rectangle is not a square but has four sides."],"answer":"(a) valid (b) valid (c) fallacy (d) fallacy","figs":[]},{"title":"Testing a chain argument","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Use a truth table to show that the argument “$p\\rightarrow q$, $q\\rightarrow r$; therefore $p\\rightarrow r$” is valid. Then apply it: “If the Black Stars train hard, they win. If they win, they qualify.”"}],"steps":["Build the table:",{"table":{"k":"table","head":["$p$","$q$","$r$","$p\\rightarrow q$","$q\\rightarrow r$","$p\\rightarrow r$"],"rows":[["T","T","T","T","T","T"],["T","T","F","T","F","F"],["T","F","T","F","T","T"],["T","F","F","F","T","F"],["F","T","T","T","T","T"],["F","T","F","T","F","T"],["F","F","T","T","T","T"],["F","F","F","T","T","T"]]}},"Both premises are true in rows 1, 5, 7 and 8.","In each of these rows $p\\rightarrow r$ is true, so the argument is **valid**.","Application: “If the Black Stars train hard, they qualify.”"],"answer":"Valid; conclusion: if they train hard, they qualify.","figs":[]},{"title":"Short, cruel and intelligent men","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$x$: There is no short man who is cruel. $y$: Some cruel men are intelligent. Draw a Venn diagram with $U$ = men, $S$ = short men, $C$ = cruel men and $I$ = intelligent men. Decide whether each is a valid conclusion. (i) Yaw is a short man, so Yaw is not intelligent. (ii) Kwame is a short and intelligent man, so Kwame is not cruel. (iii) Kofi is tall, so Kofi is cruel but not intelligent."}],"steps":["$x$: $S\\cap C=\\varnothing$. $y$: $C\\cap I\\neq\\varnothing$. Nothing says whether $S$ and $I$ meet, so the diagram allows it.","(i) The statements do not link $S$ with $I$: Yaw may or may not be intelligent. **Not valid**.","(ii) Kwame $\\in S$ and $S\\cap C=\\varnothing$, so Kwame $\\notin C$. **Valid** (his intelligence is irrelevant).","(iii) Being outside $S$ tells us nothing about $C$ or $I$. **Not valid**."],"answer":"(i) not valid (ii) valid (iii) not valid","figs":["w02-cruel"]},{"title":"Subject combinations","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a certain school: $S$: students who do Elective Science do Additional Mathematics. $R$: students who do Additional Mathematics do not do subject $C$. Let $E$, $M$ and $C$ be the sets of students who take Elective Science, Additional Mathematics and subject $C$. (a) Write $S$ and $R$ in symbols. (b) Decide whether each is valid: (i) Esi takes Additional Mathematics, so she is a science student. (ii) Mintah does not take $C$, so he is not a science student. (iii) Fio is a science student, so Fio does not take $C$."}],"steps":["(a) $S$: $E\\rightarrow M$ ($E\\subset M$). $R$: $M\\rightarrow C'$ ($M\\cap C=\\varnothing$). By the chain rule, $E\\rightarrow C'$.","(b)(i) This is the converse $M\\rightarrow E$: affirming the consequent. **Not valid**: Esi may be in $M$ outside $E$.","(ii) This is $C'\\rightarrow E'$, the inverse of $E\\rightarrow C'$. Mintah could still be in $E$. **Not valid**.","(iii) $E\\rightarrow M\\rightarrow C'$: **valid**."],"answer":"(a) $E\\rightarrow M$, $M\\rightarrow C'$ (b) (i) not valid (ii) not valid (iii) valid","figs":["w02-subjects"]},{"title":"Farmers and idle people","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$p$: All farmers are hardworking. $q$: No idle person is hardworking. Decide whether each is a valid conclusion: (i) All farmers are not idle people (that is, no farmer is idle). (ii) Farmers who are idle are not hardworking. (iii) Kudjo is hardworking, so he is a farmer."}],"steps":["$p$: $F\\subset H$. $q$: $I\\cap H=\\varnothing$. Hence $F\\cap I=\\varnothing$.","(i) No farmer can be in $I$: **valid**.","(ii) Anyone idle is outside $H$ by $q$, so an idle farmer would not be hardworking. The statement follows from $q$, so it is **valid**; but by (i) there are no idle farmers at all, so it says nothing useful.","(iii) $H$ may contain people other than farmers: affirming the consequent, **not valid**."],"answer":"(i) valid (ii) valid (but describes an empty set) (iii) not valid","figs":["w02-farmers"]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Test conjectures: constant first differences give a linear rule, constant second differences a quadratic rule. One counterexample destroys a conjecture.","A decision is logical when options are compared on stated factors; weighted score $=\\sum(\\text{weight}\\times\\text{rating})$.","$p\\rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is T and $q$ is F.","$p\\rightarrow q\\equiv\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$ (contrapositive); the converse and inverse are not equivalent to it.","Valid: modus ponens, modus tollens, chain, disjunctive. Fallacies: affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent.","An argument is valid if the conclusion is true in every row where all premises are true."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"The next term of $1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \\dots$ is","options":["21","18","20","26"],"correct":0,"explain":"Each term is the sum of the two before: $8+13=21$."},{"q":"The $n$th term of $1, 3, 6, 10, \\dots$ is","options":["$\\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$","$2n-1$","$n^2-1$","$\\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Check: $n=4$ gives $\\dfrac{4\\times5}{2}=10$."},{"q":"$p\\rightarrow q$ is false when","options":["$p$ is true and $q$ is false","$p$ is false and $q$ is true","both are false","both are true"],"correct":0,"explain":"A promise is broken only when the condition holds and the result does not."},{"q":"The contrapositive of “If it is a mango tree, then it bears fruit” is","options":["If it does not bear fruit, then it is not a mango tree.","If it bears fruit, then it is a mango tree.","If it is not a mango tree, then it does not bear fruit.","It is a mango tree and it does not bear fruit."],"correct":0,"explain":"The contrapositive is $\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$."},{"q":"Which statement is equivalent to $p\\rightarrow q$?","options":["$\\sim q\\rightarrow\\sim p$","$q\\rightarrow p$","$\\sim p\\rightarrow\\sim q$","$p\\wedge q$"],"correct":0,"explain":"A conditional and its contrapositive always agree."},{"q":"“If Ama is in Kumasi, she is in Ghana. Ama is in Ghana. So Ama is in Kumasi.” This argument is","options":["invalid: it affirms the consequent","valid: modus ponens","valid: modus tollens","invalid: it denies the antecedent"],"correct":0,"explain":"Ama could be in Accra."},{"q":"“If the light is on, someone is home. No one is home. So the light is off.” This is","options":["modus tollens, valid","modus ponens, valid","affirming the consequent, invalid","denying the antecedent, invalid"],"correct":0,"explain":"$p\\rightarrow q$, $\\sim q$, therefore $\\sim p$."},{"q":"A tank gains 120 litres and loses 5 litres each day. How many days are needed to fill 2300 litres?","options":["20","19","21","23"],"correct":0,"explain":"Net gain 115 litres a day; $2300\\div115=20$ exactly."},{"q":"“No reptile has fur. Some pets are reptiles.” Which conclusion is valid?","options":["Some pets do not have fur.","No pet has fur.","All pets are reptiles.","Some reptiles have fur."],"correct":0,"explain":"The pets that are reptiles have no fur."},{"q":"A compound statement that is true in every row of its truth table is called","options":["a tautology","a contradiction","a converse","an open sentence"],"correct":0,"explain":"For example $p\\vee\\sim p$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Find the next two terms and the $n$th term of $5, 9, 13, 17, \\dots$","a":"21, 25; $T_n=4n+1$"},{"q":"Find the next two terms and the $n$th term of $3, 8, 15, 24, 35, \\dots$","a":"48, 63; $T_n=n^2+2n=n(n+2)$"},{"q":"Is 399 a term of the sequence in question 2? If so, which term?","a":"Yes: $n(n+2)=399$ gives $n=19$"},{"q":"Test the conjecture “$2^n+1$ is prime for every positive integer $n$.”","a":"False: $n=3$ gives 9"},{"q":"A 9000-litre tank receives 250 litres a day and loses 10 litres a day. On which day is it full?","a":"$9000\\div240=37.5$: full on day 38"},{"q":"Write the converse, inverse and contrapositive of “If a triangle is equilateral, then it is isosceles.” State which are true.","a":"Converse: if isosceles then equilateral (F). Inverse: if not equilateral then not isosceles (F). Contrapositive: if not isosceles then not equilateral (T)."},{"q":"Construct a truth table for $\\sim p\\rightarrow q$ and compare it with $p\\vee q$.","a":"Identical columns: T, T, T, F"},{"q":"Is the argument “$p\\vee q$; $\\sim q$; therefore $p$” valid? Justify with a truth table.","a":"Valid: the only row with both premises true has $p$ true"},{"q":"Name the form and decide validity: “If you are a Ghanaian citizen, you can vote at 18. Esi cannot vote at 18. So Esi is not a Ghanaian citizen.”","a":"Modus tollens: valid in form (if the premise is true)"},{"q":"$p$: All engineers are good at mathematics. $q$: Some good mathematicians are teachers. Is “Some engineers are teachers” a valid conclusion?","a":"Not valid: the teachers may lie outside the engineers"},{"q":"A trader can sell 60 crates of eggs in her village at GH₵58 each, or at a city market at GH₵66 each with transport of GH₵4 a crate and a toll of GH₵150. Which is better, and by how much?","a":"Village GH₵3480; city GH₵3810 − 150 = GH₵3570 net of transport and toll (66 − 4 = 62 a crate): city by GH₵90"},{"q":"Using weights 0.5 for cost and 0.5 for speed, compare okada (cost 8, speed 9) and taxi (cost 4, speed 7) for a short trip through heavy traffic.","a":"Okada 8.5, taxi 5.5: okada (safety should also be weighed)"}],"theory":[{"q":"(a) Show that $1+3+5+\\dots+(2n-1)$ appears to equal $n^2$ by checking $n=1$ to $5$. (b) Use the dot-square picture or pairing to explain why the result is always true. (c) Hence find $1+3+5+\\dots+99$.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $1=1^2$, $1+3=4=2^2$, $1+3+5=9=3^2$, $1+3+5+7=16=4^2$, $1+3+5+7+9=25=5^2$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) A square of $n\\times n$ dots grows into an $(n+1)\\times(n+1)$ square by adding an L-shaped border of $n+(n+1)=2n+1$ dots, which is the next odd number. Alternatively pair the first and last terms: there are $n$ terms with average $\\dfrac{1+(2n-1)}{2}=n$, so the sum is $n\\times n=n^2$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $2n-1=99$ gives $n=50$, so the sum is $50^2=2500$."}]},{"q":"(a) Copy and complete a truth table for $p$, $q$, $p\\rightarrow q$, $\\sim p$ and $\\sim p\\vee q$. (b) What do you conclude? (c) Use your result to write “If you are late, you will be punished” as an “or” statement.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a)"},{"k":"table","head":["$p$","$q$","$p\\rightarrow q$","$\\sim p$","$\\sim p\\vee q$"],"rows":[["T","T","T","F","T"],["T","F","F","F","F"],["F","T","T","T","T"],["F","F","T","T","T"]]},{"k":"p","text":"(b) The columns for $p\\rightarrow q$ and $\\sim p\\vee q$ are identical, so $p\\rightarrow q\\equiv\\sim p\\vee q$."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) “You are not late, or you will be punished.”"}]},{"q":"Your school has funds for four new facilities: a science laboratory, an e-learning library, an athletics field and a 300-bed dormitory, to be placed in four zones $Z_1$–$Z_4$. Conditions: (1) the field must be in $Z_4$, the only large flat zone; (2) the library must not be next to the field (noise); (3) the dormitory must be next to the field; (4) the laboratory must not be in $Z_1$, which floods. The zones are in a row $Z_1$–$Z_2$–$Z_3$–$Z_4$. Find the placement and justify each step.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"Step 1: by (1), field $=Z_4$."},{"k":"p","text":"Step 2: by (3), the dormitory is next to $Z_4$, so dormitory $=Z_3$."},{"k":"p","text":"Step 3: $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ remain for the library and laboratory. By (4) the laboratory is not in $Z_1$, so laboratory $=Z_2$ and library $=Z_1$."},{"k":"p","text":"Step 4: check (2): the library in $Z_1$ is not next to the field in $Z_4$ ✓."},{"k":"p","text":"Placement: $Z_1$ library, $Z_2$ laboratory, $Z_3$ dormitory, $Z_4$ field. Each step was forced by a condition, so the solution is unique."}]},{"q":"Adwoa grew flowers in a store room; their leaves were deep green and healthy. Danso argued: “Sunshine supports plant growth, so Adwoa’s report must be false.” Analyse the validity of Danso’s argument.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"Danso’s argument has the form: “Sunshine supports growth (premise). So the plants could not have withered in the open (conclusion).” The conclusion does not follow, because the premise is a general tendency, not a rule that holds in every case."},{"k":"p","text":"Possible explanations that keep Adwoa’s report true: (1) the store room may have had enough light (a window or electric light); (2) the sudden change to strong sun can scorch shade-grown leaves; (3) plants in the open may have received less water, been exposed to pests or wind, or been in poor soil."},{"k":"p","text":"So Danso has not shown the report is false; his argument is invalid. A fair test would compare plants under controlled conditions."}]},{"q":"A debate motion reads: “Ghana’s natural resources should be developed using mathematical modelling rather than to meet immediate economic needs.” (a) Write the main claim as an implication $p\\rightarrow q$.
